subtitleEn: Everyone who sanctifies the seventh day
progression: | Am Am | Dm Am | E E | Am Am |
metaLine: 100 BPM · 4/4 · Friday night, usually the first zemer of the meal · eight stanzas of four lines, each stanza on its own rhyme, and the acrostic runs through the alphabet
intro: The longest of the Friday night zemirot and usually the first one sung, before the food arrives. Eight stanzas, each rhyming on a single sound, and the opening letters run through the alphabet — this is an acrostic poem of the kind the psalms use, stretched over a table song. Its subject is not the Sabbath in the abstract but the people who keep it: almost every stanza names a class of person and says what they do.

stanzas.label: whoever keeps it

lines.en: Everyone who sanctifies the seventh day as befits it,
everyone who guards the Sabbath properly from profaning it,
his reward is very great, according to his deed:
each man in his camp, and each man by his banner.

stanzas.summary: {{3.0}} through {{3.5}} is from Numbers, where the tribes camp each under its own standard. The poem borrows it to say that the reward is individual — everyone in their own place, not one reward for the crowd.

stanzas.label: those who love

lines.en: Lovers of the LORD, who wait for the building of the Temple,
on the Sabbath day be glad and rejoice, like those receiving a gift from God;
lift up your hands in holiness too, and say to God:
blessed is the LORD, who has given rest to His people Israel.

stanzas.summary: {{7.0}} through {{7.6}} is Solomon's blessing at the dedication of the Temple, in Kings. The stanza opens on people waiting for that building and closes on the words spoken when it stood.

stanzas.label: those who seek

lines.en: Those who seek the LORD, the seed of Abraham who loved Him,
who delay in leaving the Sabbath and hurry to enter it,
and are glad to keep it and to prepare its eruv:
this is the day the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.

stanzas.summary: {{9.0}} and {{9.4}} are opposites in one line — those who are slow to let the day end and quick to let it begin. That pair is the whole attitude the poem is recommending, in two words.

stanzas.label: the bride

lines.en: Remember the Torah of Moses in the commandment of the Sabbath, well studied,
engraved for the seventh day, like a bride adorned among her companions;
the pure inherit it and make it holy, by the word of Him who made everything,
and God finished on the seventh day the work that He had done.

stanzas.summary: {{13.3}} — like a bride — is the image Lecha Dodi builds a whole poem on, and here it is one word in passing. {{15.0}} through {{15.6}} is Genesis 2:2 verbatim, the verse recited over the Friday night cup.

stanzas.label: all Israel

lines.en: It is a holy day, from its coming in to its going out;
all the seed of Jacob will honour it, as the king said and decreed;
to rest on it and to be glad in the pleasure of eating and drinking:
the whole congregation of Israel will do it.

stanzas.summary: {{16.3}} and {{16.5}} mark the day by its edges — its coming in and its going out — the same phrase Menucha VeSimcha uses, and still the ordinary Hebrew for when Shabbat starts and ends.

stanzas.label: draw out Your kindness

lines.en: Draw out Your kindness to those who know You, jealous and avenging God;
to those who keep the seventh day, remembering and guarding, to establish it;
gladden them with a whole building; may the light of Your face make them shine;
they will be filled from the richness of Your house, and You will give them Your stream of delights to drink.
glosses: You will give them to drink

stanzas.summary: {{23.0}} through {{23.5}} is Psalm 36, two verses run together. {{21.3}} and {{21.4}} are the two verbs of the fourth commandment again, remember and keep, which turn up in almost every zemer on this site.

stanzas.label: help those who rest

lines.en: Help those who rest on the seventh day, in ploughing and in harvest, for ever;
who take small steps on it, who dine on it, blessing three times;
may their righteousness shine like the light of the seven days.
LORD, God of Israel, give wholeness;

stanzas.summary: {{25.2}} and {{25.3}} — a small step — is a detail from the Talmud about how one walks on Shabbat, and {{25.7}} names the three meals. The stanza is the most practical in the poem, and it is also the one with a line about ploughing and harvest, which is where the sabbatical year is hiding.

stanzas.label: eternal salvation

lines.en: LORD, God of Israel, everlasting salvation:
sanctify them by Your commandments and purify them, like the very substance of the heavens for purity;
may Your spirit give them rest, as cattle in the valley go down from the mountain;
settle their tribes in the inheritance of the moon,
planted like streams, like gardens beside a river.

stanzas.summary: {{30.2}} through {{30.6}} is Isaiah 63 and {{32.0}} through {{32.4}} is Balaam's blessing in Numbers 24, so the poem ends on two of the most visual passages in the Tanakh. Five lines rather than four: the last stanza runs long, which is normal for an acrostic that has to reach the end of the alphabet.

chantTips: Long. Eight stanzas is more than most tables sing, and stopping after three or four is completely normal.
Each stanza has its own rhyme, and the rhyme changes when the stanza does. That is your signal that a new one has started.
Around 100 BPM, and it is usually the first zemer of the evening, sung before the food comes out while everyone still has breath.
Unlike Tzur Mishelo there is no refrain, so a guest cannot join halfway. Listen through one stanza before trying.

about.body: The opening letters run through the alphabet, which is the form of several psalms and of Eshet Chayil. Over eight stanzas it acts as a memory aid for the singer and as a formal constraint on the poet, who has to find a word for each letter that also fits the stanza's rhyme.

about.h: About people, not about the day
about.body: Almost every stanza opens by naming a class of person — whoever sanctifies, lovers of the LORD, those who seek, the pure, those who rest. The poem is a description of a community rather than of a calendar, which is unusual among the zemirot.

Numbers, Kings, Genesis 2, Psalm 36, Psalm 118, Isaiah 63, Balaam's blessing. None marked. Reading the page slowly, a learner will meet half a dozen verses they already know embedded in lines that are not otherwise familiar.
